analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15, then $20 by 2029, and indexes it to median wages.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $20 an hour by 2029 was introduced September 3, 2026, referred to committee, and has no cosponsors; no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill raises the federal minimum wage in steps: $15 an hour on January 1, 2027, $17.50 in 2028, and $20 in 2029. After that, it would rise automatically each year along with the growth in the median hourly wage, so Congress would no longer have to act to keep it from falling behind the cost of living. The federal minimum has been $7.25 since 2009. The bill was introduced late in the session with a single sponsor, sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, and has seen no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers now earning between $7.25 and the new minimum—disproportionately restaurant, retail, care, and service workers—get direct raises in 2027, 2028, and 2029. After that, the automatic indexing ties the wage floor to median wage growth instead of congressional action.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15.00 an hour beginning January 1, 2027.
Raises it further to $17.50 an hour in 2028 and $20.00 an hour in 2029.

Beginning in 2030, the Secretary of Labor would raise the minimum each year by the annual percentage increase in the median hourly wage of all employees, as measured by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, so the floor tracks typical pay instead of waiting for Congress to act.
Each year's new rate must be at least as high as the rate then in effect, and is rounded to the nearest five cents.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay wages at or near the current federal minimum—restaurant and food service chains, retailers, and other low-wage service businesses—bear the higher payroll cost. Some of that cost may show up in prices or reduced hours; the workers who get the raise gain more than they pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers in food service and retail

drawbacks.text: The schedule is a steep jump: the federal minimum has been $7.25 since 2009, and this bill would roughly double it to $15 within three months of taking effect, then reach $20 by 2029. Employers with thin margins, especially small restaurants and retailers, would have to absorb the cost through prices, hours, staffing, or automation.

The bill amends the general minimum wage section of the Fair Labor Standards Act but does not change the separate lower cash wage for tipped workers, so tipped employees would not be covered by the full increase under this bill.
The indexing formula moves the wage with the median hourly wage, not with the cost of living, so in years when median pay grows slowly the minimum could still lose ground to inflation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and direct: workers making the federal minimum would see their pay roughly double within three years, with raises guaranteed annually thereafter. The cost falls on the businesses that pay those wages, some of which would raise prices or trim hours. A faster phase-in would soften the shock to small employers, and the bill leaves tipped workers outside the increase. On balance, the gains to low-wage workers are the headline effect and the costs are real but narrower.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on September 3, 2026 and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat with no further action and no vote scheduled; the current session of Congress ends January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Norma Torres introduced the Better Pay for American Workers Act in the House on September 3, 2026.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce, which decides whether the bill gets a hearing or a vote.
As of the latest record, no other member has cosponsored the bill and the committee has taken no further action on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome has been reached yet. As long as the bill stays in committee with the session ending January 3, 2027, the employers who pay the federal minimum wage are better off than they would be if it became law.

for.name: Rep. Norma Torres
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 3, 2026 to raise the federal minimum wage to $20 an hour by 2029 with automatic indexing.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no members have taken a recorded position beyond the single Democratic sponsor; the bill has zero cosponsors.

industries.note: Restaurants employ a large share of federal-minimum-wage workers, so a $15-to-$20 floor directly raises their payroll costs; their interest in keeping the floor low runs against workers' raises.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Retailers and similar businesses would face higher wage bills each year through 2029 and would likely offset some of it through prices or staffing decisions.
Workers earning between $7.25 and $20 an hour receive direct pay increases, and the indexing formula keeps the floor rising with typical wages without further votes.

analysis.trajectory: The session ends January 3, 2027, about four months after introduction. With zero cosponsors, no committee action, and no hearing scheduled, the bill will almost certainly expire in committee like most minimum-wage bills; the House Education and Workforce Committee has not advanced a federal minimum wage increase in recent sessions.
